images.caption:
Calico, a ghost town located in Yermo halfway between Los Angeles and Las Vegas, was once a very productive silver mining town, home to over 3,000 people in the 1880s. The decline in silver prices killed the mines in 1896, and the town shriveled to nothing. Today's Calico is a 1950s reconstruction by Walter Knott (of Knott's Berry Farm in Buena Park) on top of the original building foundations, donated to the County of San Bernardino in 1967.

I am on the Calico & Odessa Railroad. I am looking up at some leftover mounds from the once-productive mines of Calico. At current prices, it is estimated that assaying those mounds would yield a sizable amount of silver, worth $6 million. However, the cost of the processing would be $10 million. Declining silver prices and the resulting poor economics is what killed this town in 1896.

images.caption:
Calico, a ghost town located in Yermo halfway between Los Angeles and Las Vegas, was once a very productive silver mining town, home to over 3,000 people in the 1880s. The decline in silver prices killed the mines in 1896, and the town shriveled to nothing. Today's Calico is a 1950s reconstruction by Walter Knott (of Knott's Berry Farm in Buena Park) on top of the original building foundations, donated to the County of San Bernardino in 1967.

I am on the Calico & Odessa Railroad, which has brought me to the site of East Calico. Well removed from the saloons and the brothels lining Main Street, East Calico was the "family-friendly"  part of town, safe for women and children, and home to up to 85 families. But as the mines closed in 1896 and the town decayed, East Calico has disappeared without a trace. The white wall foundation at the bottom of the hill, in the left portion of this photograph, is the last remaining trace of East Calico.

images.caption:
Calico, a ghost town located in Yermo halfway between Los Angeles and Las Vegas, was once a very productive silver mining town, home to over 3,000 people in the 1880s. The decline in silver prices killed the mines in 1896, and the town shriveled to nothing. Today's Calico is a 1950s reconstruction by Walter Knott (of Knott's Berry Farm in Buena Park) on top of the original building foundations, donated to the County of San Bernardino in 1967.

Here is a mine entrance. Calico was a productive mining town for only 15 years - 1881 to 1896. And the reconstructed mine entrance's sign tells it all; Rhyolite is located in Nevada, and well to the north of Calico. Today, due to the danger of collapse, all abandoned mines are off-limits to the public, except for Maggie Mine, which is one of the key attractions of today's reconstructed Calico.

images.caption:
Calico, a ghost town located in Yermo halfway between Los Angeles and Las Vegas, was once a very productive silver mining town, home to over 3,000 people in the 1880s. The decline in silver prices killed the mines in 1896, and the town shriveled to nothing. Today's Calico is a 1950s reconstruction by Walter Knott (of Knott's Berry Farm in Buena Park) on top of the original building foundations, donated to the County of San Bernardino in 1967.

From the vista point on top of town, I am looking east toward the site of East Calico. Removed from the saloons and the brothels of the main section of town, East Calico was the "family-friendly" part of town, once hosting up to 85 homes. Today, the foundation of a single wall is all that remains of East Calico.
